lines.text: - asham describing guilt as an accumulating load borne by the guilty party: 'bear their guilt' (Ps 5:10 imperative against the wicked; Hos 13:16 as consequence of rebellion; Hos 10:2 tied to false-hearted idol worship).

- asham noun (asham, 'guilt offering') names both the abstract wrong and the specific animal sacrifice that remedies it — the same lexical item covers offense and its cultic answer. Ten occurrences, overwhelmingly procedural (Lev 5:7, 7:5, 14:21, 19:21; 2Kgs 12:16; 1Sam 6:17's Philistine guilt offering).

- nasa (to lift/bear) in its guilt-bearing sub-sense: the guilty party bears their own iniquity as a direct, personal consequence — the formula 'he shall bear his iniquity' recurs across the unintentional-sin law (Lev 5:1, 5:17, 17:16) and the illicit-relations law (Lev 20:17, 20:19; Num 5:31), each tying the bearing directly to the specific offense just named.

- nasa applied to the Servant: 'he bore the sin of many' — the same substitutionary-bearing structure as the scapegoat (Lev 16:22), now applied to a person rather than an animal, at the same verse (Isa 53:12) already carrying H0817's 'offering for guilt' (53:10) and family G/D's transgression/iniquity vocabulary (53:5).

- Both occurrences render asham as 'condemned' rather than 'guilty' — describing the wicked being condemned (v.21) contrasted with those who take refuge in the Lord not being condemned (v.22). The English surface shifts the register from an internal state ('guilty') to a forensic outcome ('condemned'), and the verse pairing itself frames guilt/condemnation as the fate specifically avoided by refuge in God, not merely an abstract state.

- Surface rendering 'suffer' (flocks of sheep suffering for lack of pasture) — a further occurrence of asham's alternate 'be desolate/suffer' sense (Niphal), applied to livestock, with no moral content. Between this and Ezek 6:6, at least 2 of asham's 30 occurrences carry the 'desolate/suffer' sense rather than 'be guilty' — roughly 7% of this strong's occurrences are a different word-sense than the family's own name implies.

- Two occurrences use nasa without any guilt/iniquity/punishment object at all: Ezek 16:52's 'bear your disgrace' (shame, not guilt) and Prov 19:19's 'pay the penalty' for a man of great wrath. These extend the same lift/bear/carry verb to shame and to a financial-penalty sense respectively — evidence that the guilt-bearing reading is one of several live objects this verb can take, not an inherent property of the verb itself.

- The identical 'realizes his guilt' formula, applied to progressively different classes of offender/offense (the whole congregation, a leader, a commoner, one who touches something unclean, a rash oath, and the guilt-offering procedure itself), recurs across Lev 4:13, 4:22, 4:27, 5:2, 5:3, 5:4, 5:5, 5:17, 6:4 — nine occurrences, one grouped reading: the formula is a fixed legal hinge-phrase, not nine independent statements.

- Across enochos's 7 verses (9 span occurrences), the word spans from a fully literal 'held/bound' sense (Heb 2:15, bondage to fear) to a fully forensic 'liable to penalty X' sense (Matt 5:21-22, 26:66, Mark 3:29, Jas 2:10) to a cultic-propriety sense (1Cor 11:27). This is not one meaning applied uniformly — it is one root image (being held/bound) realised in three distinct registers depending on what is doing the holding: a legal system, a psychological state, or a sacred practice.

- asham's surface rendering in Lev 5:7 is 'sin' (not 'guilt' or 'guilt offering'), in a verse listing sin-offering and burnt-offering alongside it — showing the same Hebrew guilt-offering vocabulary sits directly beside, and is translated interchangeably with, the separate chattah ('sin offering') system documented in family B — the two offering-systems' vocabulary is not kept lexically distinct in the English rendering even where the underlying Hebrew terms differ.

- Ezekiel 18:19-20 uses the identical verb (nasa, 'suffer/bear') to state the opposite direction of transfer from Lev 16:22 and Isa 53:12: 'the son shall not [bear/suffer for] the iniquity of the father' — explicitly denying transferability of guilt between generations, in the same lexical family that elsewhere affirms substitutionary transfer (scapegoat, Servant). The data does not resolve this tension; both uses are equally attested by the same word.

- Isaiah 53 is cited by three of this family's strongs at once (H0817 v.10, H5375J v.12, and via family G/D's independent citations of v.5) — the Servant Song functions as a convergence point across at least three separately-catalogued gloss-families in this cluster, not a coincidence of one family's reading.

- The guilt-offering vocabulary (H0817, H0819) sits directly beside, and in Lev 5:7 is translated interchangeably with, the sin-offering vocabulary catalogued separately as family B (chattah) — worth checking whether these two offering-systems should be read together rather than as separate families, given how closely the English surface conflates them.

- Jer 51:5's 'full of guilt' (H0817) uses the same 'filled with X' construction found in family F's chamas ('the earth was filled with violence,' Gen 6:11/13) — a recurring figure across this cluster describing a wrong as reaching a saturation point in a place or people, not merely an individual act.
